Promotions are the largest lever: returning to their FY2023 share would add about $9.9M a year

slides.title: Why the margin fell
Gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment, not store labor, explain 79% of the margin decline since FY2023

claims.claim: 79% of the margin decline comes from gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment
evidence: Chart: FY2023 margin 3.37%; Gross margin step 1.019%; Store labor 0.2996%; Occupancy and energy 0.1985%; E-commerce fulfillment 0.8381%; Other SG&A 0.0001%; FY2025 margin 1.02%

claims.claim: Gross margin: 43% of the decline, from heavier promotions and rising shrink
E-commerce fulfillment: 36%, as picking and delivery costs grew far faster than online sales
Store labor: only 13%, the driver management's plan is built on
Occupancy and SG&A: occupancy explains 8%; other SG&A held at 4.7% of sales

slides.title: Promotions and shrink drove the gross-margin loss, which private label offset by only 0.18 percentage points

claims.claim: Promotions and shrink are fixable; private label is the lever to scale
evidence: Chart: FY2023 gross margin 26.04%; More promotional sales −0.7 pp; Higher shrink −0.5 pp; More private label +0.18 pp; FY2025 gross margin 25.02%

claims.claim: Promotions: the promotional share rose from 24% to 29% of sales, and vendors now fund only 46% of markdowns, against 55%
Shrink: rose from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales as stores ran with fewer hours
Private label: its gain offset only 15% of the promotion and shrink loss
Expected gain if private label keeps its FY2023–25 pace to FY2028: $3.8M
evidence: 0.18 pp in two years, repeated for three more years, × $1,412M FY2028 sales
promotional sales: 14 pp below regular price; private label: 12 pp above national brands

slides.title: Fewer hours per sales dollar absorbed most of the 9.4% wage rise, leaving store labor only 0.3 percentage points higher

claims.claim: Wage inflation was real
evidence: 9.4% average hourly wage incl. benefits, FY2023 to FY2025
From $16.80 to $18.38 an hour
State minimum wage and a tight labor market (CFO and COO)
At FY2023 hours, it alone would have added 1.11 percentage points of sales

claims.claim: Productivity offset about 70% of it
evidence: −6% labor hours per $1,000 of sales
From 7.02 to 6.60 hours per $1,000 of sales
Stores already run leaner than in FY2023
Stores with the fewest hours skip produce rotation and receiving checks

claims.claim: A minor driver of the margin decline
evidence: 0.3 pp change in store labor as a share of sales
From 11.8% to 12.1% of sales
13% of the 2.35-percentage-point margin decline

claims.claim: Cutting hours further attacks the smallest driver

slides.title: Why not cut store hours
Thin staffing shows up as shrink: the least-staffed quarter of stores loses 3.1% of sales, against 2.3% for the best-staffed

claims.claim: Staffing protects the fresh offer that brings shoppers in
evidence: Chart: shrink % of sales FY2025 — Q1 fewest hours 3.1%; Q2 2.7%; Q3 2.4%; Q4 most hours 2.3%
Chain average 2.6%

claims.claim: Q1 stores: managers say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days
fresh waste (45%) and receiving errors (20%) are 65% of shrink, both tied to store tasks
Q4 stores: prove 2.3% is reachable inside today's network
Expected gain if the chain matched the best-staffed quartile: $4.2M

slides.title: The proposed 8% hour cut could give back up to $10M of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink

claims.claim: The proposed 8% hour cut could give back up to $10M of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink
evidence: $14.5M a year from cutting scheduled store hours by 8% (management estimate)
$10M a year of extra shrink: 0.5 pp rise per 6.0% fewer hours in FY2023–25, scaled to 8%, × $1,503M sales
$4.5M net saving left, before any loss of shoppers to longer checkout waits or stock-outs

claims.claim: If only waste and receiving errors (65% of shrink) respond to hours, the loss is about $6.5M
Even with no shrink effect, the cut lifts FY2028 margin only to about 2.0%, short of the 3.0% target

slides.title: Promotions are the largest lever: returning to their FY2023 share would add about $9.9M a year
Heavier promotions have not bought a cheaper image: promotional sales reached 29% as 'more expensive' ratings rose to 41%

claims.claim: Promotions now carry nearly a third of sales
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional share: FY2023 24%; FY2024 26.2%; FY2025 29%

claims.claim: Yet more shoppers see Harlow as expensive
evidence: +8 pp
Say Harlow is more expensive: FY2023 33%; FY2025 41%
Customer survey, n = 3,100

claims.claim: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money even after counting the extra units they sold
The category team's finding that the deepest-promotion stores grew comparable sales 1.8%, against 0.2%, measures sales, not profit

slides.title: ValuMart is taking sales near its new stores, but shoppers come to Harlow for fresh produce and convenience

claims.claim: Stores near the 11 new ValuMarts are losing sales
evidence: Comparable sales growth FY2025: Within 3 miles of a new ValuMart −4.2%; Other Harlow stores 1.1%
ValuMart has opened 11 stores in Harlow trade areas since 2023

claims.claim: Fresh produce and convenience are why shoppers choose Harlow
evidence: Top reasons to shop Harlow FY2025: Fresh produce 58%; Convenience 44%
Customer survey, n = 3,100

claims.claim: Defend traffic with fresh produce and convenience, not by matching a discounter's promotional depth

slides.title: Bringing promotions back to their FY2023 share of sales would add about $9.9M a year, the largest single lever

claims.claim: Bringing promotions back to their FY2023 share of sales would add about $9.9M a year
evidence: 5 pp less promotional share of sales, back to the FY2023 level of 24% (from 29%)
× 14 pp less gross margin on each promotional dollar than at regular price (category data)
× $1,412M Harlow sales in FY2028, after the store exits and delivery fee change
= $9.9M more gross profit a year; removes 17% of promotional sales

claims.claim: Cut the money-losing events first; they make up 38% of events
evidence: Cuts start with the 38% of FY2025 events that lost money even after counting extra units, so lost volume does not erode the gain

claims.claim: Vendor funding, down from 55% to 46% of markdowns, is not counted; recovering it is upside
Stores within three miles of a ValuMart keep today's promotional depth until weekly comparable sales show the cuts elsewhere held traffic

slides.title: E-commerce and weak stores
E-commerce fulfillment cost rose 3.5 times in two years, with net home-delivery cost growing fastest

claims.claim: 3.5x growth in fulfillment cost, FY2023 to FY2025
evidence: Delivery, net of fees: FY2023 $1.94M; FY2024 $4.59M; FY2025 $8.26M
totals match the income statement ($5.2M, $10.9M, $18.1M)

claims.claim: Orders: grew 2.9 times as e-commerce rose from 3.0% to 8.5% of sales
Home delivery: net cost grew 4.3 times as the delivered share rose from 45% to 58% of orders
Each delivered order: the carrier is paid $13.80 and the fee collected is $3.10, a $10.70 loss before picking
Why fees are low: delivery is free above $75, below the average basket

slides.title: Counted in full, e-commerce loses about $10.4M a year, not the profit the e-commerce team reports

claims.claim: Counted in full, e-commerce loses about $10.4M a year
evidence: $127.8M e-commerce sales, FY2025 (8.5% of sales)
× 30% share new to Harlow: 70% would otherwise be bought in a Harlow store (survey, n = 2,300)
× 20% contribution per new dollar before fulfillment (finance estimate)
− $18.1M fulfillment: picking plus third-party delivery, net of $2.4M of fees
= −$10.4M e-commerce profit a year, −8.2% of its sales

claims.claim: Two corrections turn the team's 6.1% margin into a loss
evidence: Third-party delivery is counted; the team's figure leaves it out because finance books it in e-commerce fulfillment
Only new-to-Harlow sales count; the team's figure treats every online sale as new

claims.claim: The owners' wish to keep delivery holds; the task is to stop each delivered order losing $10.70 before picking

slides.title: Rolling out the tested delivery fee would cut the e-commerce loss by about $2.8M a year and keep home delivery

claims.claim: Fewer orders ride on the carrier fee
evidence: −9% change in delivered orders
Fee $7.99, free above $100
Each one avoided saves $13.80

claims.claim: Most customers switched, not left
evidence: 14% rise in click-and-collect orders
Click-and-collect stays free
It costs only picking, $7.40

claims.claim: Fees now cover about half the carrier cost
evidence: $6.4 average fee per delivered order
Up from $3.10 in FY2025

claims.claim: Total e-commerce sales fell only 2%
evidence: Only 30% of online sales are new
Most lost sales stay in stores
Fee test: 4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025

claims.claim: $2.8M rollout gain a year, team estimate
evidence: $18.1M fulfillment cost, FY2025
− $15.1M at test terms: 703k delivered + 637k collected orders
− $0.2M contribution lost on 2% fewer sales
= $2.8M gain a year

slides.title: Exiting the nine loss-making stores would add about $6.6M a year, six of them at lease expiry

claims.claim: Exiting the nine loss-making stores would add about $6.6M a year
evidence: $3.1M four-wall EBITDA losses of the nine stores, removed
+ $118M combined sales of the nine stores, FY2025 × 25% of those sales moving to a nearby Harlow store (past closures) × 12% contribution on moved sales at the receiving store
= $6.6M gain a year, before any saving in depreciation

claims.claim: Six exits need no board vote; three need one and $7.5M
evidence: Six of the nine leases expire by the end of 2027, so those stores close without a board vote
The other three need a board vote and an estimated $7.5M one-time lease-exit cost
The $7.5M one-time cost uses 30% of the $25M plan budget

claims.claim: Four-wall EBITDA excludes depreciation, so the operating-income gain is, if anything, larger

slides.title: Plan and first actions
Together, the five actions would lift operating margin to about 3.0% by FY2028, meeting the target with little room to spare

claims.claim: the five actions would lift operating margin to about 3.0% by FY2028
evidence: Chart: FY2025 margin 1.02%; Smaller sales base +0.0656 pp; Promotions +0.7 pp; Store exits +0.4703 pp; Shrink +0.3 pp; Private label +0.27 pp; Delivery fee +0.2007 pp; FY2028 margin 3.02%
$15.3M operating income, FY2025 + $27.4M five actions, run-rate = $42.7M operating income, FY2028 ÷ $1,412M FY2028 sales after exits = 3.02% operating margin

claims.claim: Promotions carry the plan; no action needs much capital
evidence: Promotions: the largest step and needs no capital; start with the events that lose money
Store exits: six at lease expiry; three need a board vote and the plan's only one-time cost
Shrink and private label: restore produce rotation and receiving checks; keep the FY2023–25 private-label pace
Delivery fee: tested in four stores; the service stays

slides.title: Unlike the labor-cut plan, the recommended plan meets the margin target without thinning Harlow's fresh offer

claims.claim: Even keeping every dollar, the labor cut reaches about 2.0%
evidence: FY2028 operating margin: Management's draft plan about 2.0%, even if the full saving is kept; Recommended plan about 3.0%, from the five actions
Labor-plan margin = ($15.3M + $14.5M saving) ÷ $1,503M FY2025 sales, with no shrink effect

claims.claim: Labor plan's headroom may vanish
evidence: FY2026 operating income (covenant: $20M): Management's draft $29.8M on paper; about $19.8M if shrink rises as in FY2023–25; Recommended about $25M from first-wave actions

claims.claim: Fresh is the top reason to shop
evidence: Fresh produce and shrink: Management's draft — fewer hours where shrink is already highest; Recommended — produce rotation and receiving checks restored

claims.claim: Both keep delivery
evidence: Delivery service: Management's draft — frozen at today's size, still losing about $10.4M a year; Recommended — kept and repriced at tested fees

claims.claim: Within the $25M budget
evidence: One-time cost and board decisions: Management's draft none; Recommended $7.5M and a vote on three lease exits

slides.title: Delivery repricing and promotion cuts come first because they lift income fastest and keep the lender's covenant safe

claims.claim: Delivery repricing and promotion cuts come first because they lift income fastest and keep the lender's covenant safe
evidence: Roadmap H1 FY2026–H2 FY2028: Delivery fee roll out; Promotions cut losing events; Shrink restore store routines; Delivery contract tender; Store exits exit nine stores; Private label keep share gains; milestones Board vote, Covenant test, Wage +4%
$15.3M FY2025 actual + $2.1M delivery fee, about 75% of a year + $4.9M promotions, half of run-rate + $2.7M shrink and private label, a third = $25M FY2026 estimate; covenant is $20M

slides.title: The 2027 minimum-wage rise is the largest risk to the target, worth up to $7.3M a year unless productivity offsets it

claims.claim: The 2027 minimum-wage rise is the largest risk to the target, worth up to $7.3M a year unless productivity offsets it
evidence: $181.9M store labor, FY2025 × 4% minimum-wage rise, if it applied to every wage = $7.3M cost a year, before productivity offsets

State minimum wage +4% in 2027: $7.3M; Offset with scheduling gains outside produce and receiving; hold labor at 12.1% of sales; Needs an offset plan / Unoffset, it would leave FY2028 margin near 2.5%

claims.claim: Fewer sales move after store exits: measurable early
evidence: $1.4M per 10 pp less transfer ($118.0M × 10 pp × 12%)
Exit at lease expiry first and measure transfer before the three voted exits

claims.claim: Carrier's proposed 3% rate rise: small
evidence: About $0.3M (703k delivered orders × $13.80 × 3%)
Tender the contract at the 2026 renewal; the fee change already cuts delivered orders 9%

claims.claim: Promotion cuts lose traffic near ValuMart: watch weekly
evidence: Not sized
Cut losing events outside ValuMart areas first; track comparable sales weekly

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Fix promotions, shrink, delivery and weak stores, not store hours, to reach 3.0% by FY2028: approve the margin plan and vote on exiting the three stores whose leases run beyond 2027 ($7.5M); roll out the tested delivery fee; cut the money-losing promotional events; withdraw the 8% hour cut and restore produce rotation and receiving checks; exit nine loss-making stores; keep the private-label pace. Delivery repricing and promotion cuts come first.

alternatives_considered.option: Management's draft plan: 8% cut in scheduled store labor hours
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: targets the smallest driver (store labor, 13% of decline) and could give back up to $10M of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink; even with no shrink effect lifts FY2028 margin only to about 2.0%, short of the 3.0% target; FY2026 income $29.8M on paper but about $19.8M if shrink rises as in FY2023–25 (covenant headroom may vanish); fewer hours where shrink is already highest. Next step: withdraw the 8% hour cut.

alternatives_considered.option: Recommended plan (five actions: promotions, store exits, shrink, private label, delivery fee)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen: about 3.0% FY2028 margin, about $25M FY2026 income above $20M covenant, $7.5M one-time cost within the $25M budget, keeps delivery and the fresh offer.
Rejected: 'Defend traffic with fresh produce and convenience, not by matching a discounter's promotional depth'; heavier promotions have not bought a cheaper image.

alternatives_considered.option: Delivery frozen at today's size (management's draft) vs. kept and repriced at tested fees
alternatives_considered.treatment: Repricing chosen: management's draft leaves delivery losing about $10.4M a year; the tested fee ($7.99, free above $100) cuts the loss by about $2.8M and keeps home delivery, respecting the owners' wish to keep delivery.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Fictional company; synthetic benchmark data from the briefing pack
Steps are computed from the income statement and may not add to the total because of rounding

Hour-cut upper case assumes shrink tracks hours as it did in FY2023–25: all of the FY2023–25 rise in shrink (2.1% to 2.6%) is attributed to the 6.0% fall in hours per $1,000 of sales; shrink responds in proportion to hours (8% cut adds about 0.67 pp)
If only waste and receiving errors (65% of shrink) respond to hours, the shrink loss is about $6.5M
Effects on checkout waits and stock-outs are not counted
Theft, the remaining 35% of shrink, is less tied to staffing
FY2028 sales ($1,412M) assume the store exits and delivery fee change
Promotion gain: sales leaving promotion are bought at regular price, earning the 14 pp of margin promotions give up; vendor funding recovery not counted (upside)
Stores within three miles of a ValuMart keep today's promotional depth until weekly comparable sales show the cuts elsewhere held traffic; traffic loss near ValuMart is not sized
E-commerce: only 30% of online sales are new to Harlow (survey, n = 2,300); contribution of 20 cents per new dollar is a finance estimate including packaging and allocated store costs
Delivery fee rollout: carrier and picking costs per order held at FY2025 levels; based on a 4-store, 10-week test
Store exits: 25% of sales transfer to nearby Harlow stores at 12% contribution, as in past closures; $1.4M less gain per 10 pp less transfer
Phasing is a team assumption; FY2026 is treated as the first plan year, as in management's draft; FY2026 figures are team estimates
State minimum wage +4% in 2027 is the main risk, up to $7.3M a year (upper bound assuming every store wage rises 4%); unoffset, it would leave FY2028 margin near 2.5%
The plan meets the target 'with little room to spare'
next_steps: Approve the margin plan and vote on exiting the three stores whose leases run beyond 2027 ($7.5M) — Board — February 2027 meeting
Roll out the tested delivery fee ($7.99, free above $100) to all stores — Head of e-commerce — Within the first quarter of the plan
Cancel the money-losing promotional events and reopen vendor-funding talks — Category managers — Next promotional cycle
Withdraw the 8% hour cut; restore produce rotation and receiving checks in the least-staffed stores — COO — Immediately
Confirm the FY2026 covenant forecast with the lender and tender the delivery contract — CFO — Before the 2026 contract renewal
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck had no pictures; all charts came through as native chart data. I read chart values from the 'base' and value series of the waterfall charts (slides 4, 5 and 20) and converted them to percentages and percentage points. I copied one point exactly as it appears in the source: slide 4's 'Other SG&A' step is 0.0001%. The slide 22 roadmap only lists bar labels and milestone names, so the exact half-year each action falls in can't be recovered. Slide 10's section divider repeats the section headline as its title, while the other dividers use short titles.
